claims: Bounding is a multi-jump exercise commonly performed in alternate-leg, same-leg, or double-leg modes, usually with horizontal projection as a defining intent.

{{canonicalName}} must state contact sequence, takeoff and landing laterality, projection bias, continuity, number of contacts, terminal action, surface gradient, and reset; labels such as rhythm, distance, or height alone do not establish a new identity.
Horizontal multi-step jumps combine forward-directed force production with repeated unilateral contacts under temporal constraints.

{{canonicalName}} belongs to multi-contact plyometric output; alternate-leg and repeated same-leg contacts are controlled identities, while distance, height, rhythm, contact count, and measurement method are controlled variants or delivery dimensions.
Bounding coordinates rapid force production and absorption across the foot, ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, and trunk on repeated unilateral contacts.

The card should assign plantar-flexor and intrinsic-foot stiffness, knee-extensor and hip-extensor propulsion and braking, hamstring swing and stance roles, frontal-plane hip stabilization, arm action, and lumbopelvic control without reducing the task to one muscle.
Horizontally oriented plyometric training has direction-specific advantages for horizontal performance, while vertical and horizontal tasks should not be treated as mechanically interchangeable.

Observable execution must match the card: project the center of mass, strike beneath or only slightly ahead of it, resist braking and collapse, coordinate opposite arm and leg, and preserve the selected horizontal, vertical, or blended bias.
Multi-step horizontal jumps require forward force production, short contact constraints, repeated unilateral organization, and preservation of velocity across contacts.

Exercise difficulty must score technical complexity, physical and absolute-load demand, coordination, supervision, consequence of error, impact, work-capacity demand, and overall difficulty directly; projection distance or an athlete label is not an exercise difficulty score.
Plyometric exposure is meaningfully affected by total ground contacts and accumulated intervention volume, so contacts must be counted rather than hidden inside generic repetitions or work intervals.

{{canonicalName}} needs per-leg and total contacts, surface, projection intent, approach, terminal landing, technical-fatigue thresholds, inter-attempt recovery, between-set recovery, and weekly high-impact accounting.
High-intensity plyometrics require progressive preparation, adequate strength and landing control, safe equipment and surfaces, and sufficient recovery.

The delivery profile should require a long unobstructed lane, level or explicitly graded non-slip surface, suitable footwear, visible finish and run-out zones, safe athlete spacing, and coach sightlines to both frontal and sagittal mechanics.
Ground-contact volume is a programming variable and should be interpreted with intervention duration, task intensity, maturity, training history, and outcome rather than copied as a universal dose.

Prescribe attempts or lanes, contacts per attempt and per leg, distance or contact cap, projection intent, terminal action, full walk-back or timed recovery, and a quality stop; do not prescribe two-second recovery for maximal multi-contact bounds.
Sprint and jump coaches use bounding to develop horizontally directed force and acceleration-related qualities, with execution differentiated by alternate, single, or double contacts.

Use a small cue set: tall but directionally projected posture, drive through the ground, exchange opposite arm and knee, contact under the hips, keep the pelvis level, and finish with the prescribed stick or run-out.
Advanced unilateral plyometrics require technical readiness, conservative progression, appropriate supervision, and discontinuation when quality or safety deteriorates.

Stop for pain, giving way, apprehension, repeated valgus or pelvic drop, foot collapse, reaching and braking, loud contacts, loss of rhythm, unintended contact pattern, decreasing distance or velocity, unsafe lane encroachment, or an uncontrolled final landing.
Horizontal multi-step jump performance and training can relate to sprint outcomes, but transfer depends on task, population, program, and measurement context.
{{canonicalName}} belongs early in a fresh output block after landing, hopping, and lower-amplitude bounding readiness; use it to train or measure a named quality, not as conditioning volume.
Athlete support should show the exact left-right or same-leg contact pattern, the intended projection angle, arm timing, contact zone, finish, recovery, and what makes a repetition count.
Use lane markers and one outcome cue, explain the difference between rhythm and maximal-distance attempts, and show how to reduce amplitude without changing the contact sequence.
Coach support should distinguish alternate, same-leg, and double-leg bounding and select orientation according to the intended performance transfer.

Provide front and side observation, per-leg contact counts, contact-sequence diagrams, projection and braking criteria, side-to-side comparison, lane and surface setup, workload accounting, regressions, progressions, and terminal-landing rules.
Plyometric selection and progression should match physical and psychosocial readiness, technical competence, supervision, and equipment scale.

Accessibility can be improved with shorter lanes, lower amplitude, bound-and-stick contacts, visual footprints, external rhythm marks, fewer contacts, longer recovery, quieter settings, or supported single-leg landings while still assessing the exercise through its difficulty dimensions.
Horizontal and vertical plyometric orientations create meaningfully different directional demands and adaptations.

Contact pattern and surface gradient require a distinct definition or variant; height, distance, rhythm, contact count, approach length, terminal stick, and measurement intent normally belong in variant or delivery profiles unless they change the actual contact sequence.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

The direct candidates for {{canonicalName}} were discovered through visible YouTube search; current availability and embedding, exact contact pattern and projection match, complete viewing, captions, instructional quality, safety, and approval remain separate review gates.
